evidence.claim: Section 5 vests federal executive power in the President and allows exercise directly or through the Vice-President, ministers, or other officers, subject to the Constitution and National Assembly laws.
evidence.title: Nigeria 1999 (rev. 2023) Constitution
evidence.excerpt: Section 5 vests federal executive power in the President and allows exercise directly or through the Vice-President, ministers, or other officers, subject to the Constitution and National Assembly laws.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary constitutional text; the cited provision is directly visible and stable.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Buhari held this office in 2022, so the provision defines his formal authority rather than a specific action.
contrary_evidence: This does not show how Buhari used executive power in practice.

evidence.claim: Buhari said the 2022 budget was guided by 2021-2025 National Development Plan objectives including diversification, infrastructure, security, a vibrant educated and healthy populace, reducing poverty, and minimizing regional, economic, and social disparities, and he described it as intended to improve the living conditions of Nigerians.
evidence.title: 2022 Budget Speech: Budget of Economic Growth and Sustainability – President Buhari
evidence.excerpt: Buhari said the 2022 budget was guided by 2021-2025 National Development Plan objectives including diversification, infrastructure, security, a vibrant educated and healthy populace, reducing poverty, and minimizing regional, economic, and social disparities, and he described it as intended to improve the living conditions of Nigerians.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct presidential budget speech during the target year, with explicit welfare-oriented objectives and strong ruler attribution.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 budget speech in the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Buhari statement as president; strong attribution to executive intent, though not proof of implementation.
contrary_evidence: The speech is aspirational and does not by itself prove delivered welfare gains.
Nigeria still had severe poverty and human-development gaps in 2022.

evidence.claim: The 2022 budget priorities included completion of major road and rail projects, power-sector projects, potable water, irrigation infrastructure and dams, emergency medical services and ambulances, procurement of vaccines, polio eradication, and upgrades to primary health care centres across the six geopolitical zones.
evidence.title: 2022 Budget Speech: Budget of Economic Growth and Sustainability – President Buhari
evidence.excerpt: The 2022 budget priorities included completion of major road and rail projects, power-sector projects, potable water, irrigation infrastructure and dams, emergency medical services and ambulances, procurement of vaccines, polio eradication, and upgrades to primary health care centres across the six geopolitical zones.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct official budget speech with concrete program priorities tied to social and health infrastructure.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 policy statement and budget plan.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Buhari budget statement; implementation still depended on ministries and subnational delivery.
contrary_evidence: This is a plan, not outcome evidence.
The same period still shows severe shortfalls in health, water, and living conditions.

evidence.claim: Buhari said 988,652 poor and indigent Nigerians had been enrolled in the Basic Health Care Provision Fund, and that 7,373 primary health facilities had been accredited and capitated under the National Health Insurance Scheme pathway while 7,242 primary health care facilities were receiving decentralized facility financing.
evidence.title: Address By President Buhari At The 3rd Ministerial Performance Review Retreat
evidence.excerpt: Buhari said 988,652 poor and indigent Nigerians had been enrolled in the Basic Health Care Provision Fund, and that 7,373 primary health facilities had been accredited and capitated under the National Health Insurance Scheme pathway while 7,242 primary health care facilities were receiving decentralized facility financing.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Specific program and facility counts from an official presidential performance review, but still self-reported.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong attribution to federal health-policy execution, though actual delivery depended on health institutions and states.
contrary_evidence: Self-reported delivery figures may overstate service quality.
Access and quality gaps remained large nationally.

evidence.claim: The Federal Government raised the National Home Grown School Feeding Programme meal cost from N70 to N100 per child and said the change came with increased monitoring and tighter regulations.
evidence.title: National School Feeding Programme now N100 per plate
evidence.publisher: Federal Ministry of Information and National Orientation
evidence.excerpt: The Federal Government raised the National Home Grown School Feeding Programme meal cost from N70 to N100 per child and said the change came with increased monitoring and tighter regulations.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official ministry report on a specific policy change with a concrete implementation control element, but not independent evaluation.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Buhari-era federal social policy, though school feeding is implemented with state and local administrative involvement.
contrary_evidence: The article reports the funding and controls, not nutritional or enrollment outcomes.
Coverage and integrity may still vary by state and school.

evidence.claim: The Ministry of Health said the federal government had released N89 billion to the Basic Health Care Provision Fund, disbursed N56 billion to all 36 states and the FCT, and was providing operational funds to 7,250 primary health care facilities in 35 states and the FCT, aiming for at least one functional PHC in every ward.
evidence.title: BHCPF: FG DISBURSES N56 BILLION TO 36 STATES, FCT
evidence.publisher: Federal Ministry of Information and National Orientation
evidence.excerpt: The Ministry of Health said the federal government had released N89 billion to the Basic Health Care Provision Fund, disbursed N56 billion to all 36 states and the FCT, and was providing operational funds to 7,250 primary health care facilities in 35 states and the FCT, aiming for at least one functional PHC in every ward.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official ministry report with concrete disbursement and facility figures, but still an executive-side report rather than an audit.
evidence.period_fit: August 2022 target-period reporting on ongoing 2022 delivery.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Federal health-finance attribution is strong, though actual service delivery depended on state and facility execution.
contrary_evidence: Disbursement does not guarantee quality or access at point of care.
The release does not show whether all wards received functional PHCs.

evidence.claim: Nigeria, through the National Primary Health Care Development Agency with WHO support, introduced rotavirus vaccine into the routine immunization schedule; the vaccine was to be given free to infants at 6, 10, and 14 weeks and was intended to avert over 50,000 child deaths annually.
evidence.title: Nigeria to avert 50,000 deaths in children annually, introduces rotavirus vaccine into vaccination schedule
evidence.excerpt: Nigeria, through the National Primary Health Care Development Agency with WHO support, introduced rotavirus vaccine into the routine immunization schedule; the vaccine was to be given free to infants at 6, 10, and 14 weeks and was intended to avert over 50,000 child deaths annually.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: WHO news release with a clear intervention date, delivery mechanism, and health-impact rationale.
evidence.period_fit: Exact target-year health intervention dated 22 August 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong federal attribution through NPHCDA and the health ministry; rollout and uptake still depended on delivery systems.
contrary_evidence: The article does not show realized mortality reduction in 2022.
It does not establish nationwide uptake or equity of access.

evidence.claim: The NBS and UNICEF launched the 2021 MICS/NICS report as reliable nationwide and internationally comparable data to monitor the situation of children and women; the survey covered child mortality, health, nutrition, education, child and social protection, women's health, water, sanitation, hygiene, and vaccination coverage, and was explicitly meant to guide budgeting and evidence-based policy.
evidence.title: The National Bureau of Statistics in collaboration with UNICEF launches the 2021 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey/ National Immunization Coverage Survey Report
evidence.excerpt: The NBS and UNICEF launched the 2021 MICS/NICS report as reliable nationwide and internationally comparable data to monitor the situation of children and women; the survey covered child mortality, health, nutrition, education, child and social protection, women's health, water, sanitation, hygiene, and vaccination coverage, and was explicitly meant to guide budgeting and evidence-based policy.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official statistical release with direct governance-and-data language and clear target-period relevance.
evidence.period_fit: August 2022 launch of a 2021 survey used in 2022 policy work.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Buhari-era federal statistical and policy institutions, with UNICEF support; implementation and budget follow-through remain separate questions.
contrary_evidence: Measurement itself is not service improvement.
The report says progress was mixed and much remained to be done.

evidence.claim: The 2021 MICS/NICS results reported that child mortality fell from 1 in 8 children dying before age five in the 2016 survey to 1 in 10 in 2021, exclusive breastfeeding rose from 24% to 34%, birth registration rose from 47% to nearly 60%, and child marriage fell from 44% to 30%.
evidence.title: The National Bureau of Statistics in collaboration with UNICEF launches the 2021 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey/ National Immunization Coverage Survey Report
evidence.excerpt: The 2021 MICS/NICS results reported that child mortality fell from 1 in 8 children dying before age five in the 2016 survey to 1 in 10 in 2021, exclusive breastfeeding rose from 24% to 34%, birth registration rose from 47% to nearly 60%, and child marriage fell from 44% to 30%.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official survey release summarizing nationally representative results, though the gains span 2016-2021 rather than only 2022.
evidence.period_fit: Survey launched in 2022 using 2021 data; the outcomes are still relevant to the 2022 target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partial attribution only; these are broad survey outcomes shaped by multiple years, states, and partners, not a single presidential action.
contrary_evidence: The gains span several years and cannot be credited solely to Buhari in 2022.
The same release says the picture was mixed and more progress was needed.

evidence.claim: UNICEF said approximately 54% of children in Nigeria were multidimensionally poor, with rural child deprivation at 65.7% versus 28.4% in urban areas and state disparities from 14.5% in Lagos to 81.5% in Sokoto; the deprivations spanned nutrition, healthcare, education, water, sanitation, adequate housing, and information.
evidence.title: New evidence on the situation of child deprivation in Nigeria
evidence.excerpt: UNICEF said approximately 54% of children in Nigeria were multidimensionally poor, with rural child deprivation at 65.7% versus 28.4% in urban areas and state disparities from 14.5% in Lagos to 81.5% in Sokoto; the deprivations spanned nutrition, healthcare, education, water, sanitation, adequate housing, and information.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Joint UNICEF/government statistical release with explicit, target-period child deprivation figures and distributional detail.
evidence.period_fit: May 2022 release using contemporary national child-poverty analysis.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partial attribution only; the figures capture the national welfare environment under Buhari but not a clean causal estimate of his decisions.
contrary_evidence: The release is descriptive and does not separate federal from state responsibility.
It documents persistent deprivation rather than program-specific success.

evidence.claim: The World Bank said much still needed to be done to lift millions of Nigerians out of poverty, including boosting health and education, bolstering productive jobs, and expanding social protection; it also said pro-poor policy design required state-level disaggregation and stronger data.
evidence.title: Nigeria Poverty Assessment
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said much still needed to be done to lift millions of Nigerians out of poverty, including boosting health and education, bolstering productive jobs, and expanding social protection; it also said pro-poor policy design required state-level disaggregation and stronger data.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent multilateral diagnosis with a clear poverty-and-social-protection focus and explicit 2022 publication date.
evidence.period_fit: Published in March 2022, directly within the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect attribution only; this is a policy diagnosis and recommendation, not direct proof of Buhari-era delivery.
contrary_evidence: It is recommendation-heavy rather than outcome-specific.
The report does not by itself show whether Buhari implemented the suggested reforms.

evidence.claim: The World Bank said Nigeria's petrol, electricity, and foreign exchange subsidies were inefficient and regressive, were not fully visible in the budget, benefited primarily wealthy households, and crowded out spending on education, health, social protection, and pro-poor programs.
evidence.title: To Promote Inclusive and Sustainable Development, Nigeria Needs to Fix its Public Finances
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said Nigeria's petrol, electricity, and foreign exchange subsidies were inefficient and regressive, were not fully visible in the budget, benefited primarily wealthy households, and crowded out spending on education, health, social protection, and pro-poor programs.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Strong independent fiscal analysis with direct statements about distributive effects and opportunity costs.
evidence.period_fit: Published in November 2022 and squarely about 2021-2022 policy conditions.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partially attributable to Buhari-era fiscal choices, though subsidy structure also reflects inherited policy and multi-level government constraints.
contrary_evidence: The World Bank report is analytical and not a direct audit of the president's personal intent.
Some subsidy effects were inherited and macro-fiscal pressures were also external.

evidence.claim: The World Bank said rising fuel and food prices were likely to push an additional one million Nigerians into poverty by the end of 2022, and that ballooning gasoline subsidy costs were crowding out resources that were needed for children, youth, infrastructure, and jobs.
evidence.title: A 'Business Unusual' approach, even more urgently needed to reduce inflation, lessen fiscal pressures, and attract investment for jobs
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said rising fuel and food prices were likely to push an additional one million Nigerians into poverty by the end of 2022, and that ballooning gasoline subsidy costs were crowding out resources that were needed for children, youth, infrastructure, and jobs.
evidence.source_locator: lines 144-145 and surrounding press release text
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent mid-year macro-poverty estimate with explicit 2022 horizon and clear fiscal opportunity-cost language.
evidence.period_fit: June 2022 target-year estimate about end-2022 effects.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect and partial; the estimate reflects policy and shock interaction, not a clean one-person causal estimate.
contrary_evidence: The estimate is counterfactual and not observed poverty data.
Inflation was also driven by global food and fuel shocks.

evidence.claim: The IMF said the opportunity created by higher oil prices to build fiscal space and FX reserves was not harnessed, that inflation was elevated and fuel subsidies remained a formidable drain on fiscal revenues, and that Nigeria needed well-targeted social assistance to mitigate food insecurity and subsidy removal effects on the poor.
evidence.title: Nigeria: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2022 Article IV Mission
evidence.excerpt: The IMF said the opportunity created by higher oil prices to build fiscal space and FX reserves was not harnessed, that inflation was elevated and fuel subsidies remained a formidable drain on fiscal revenues, and that Nigeria needed well-targeted social assistance to mitigate food insecurity and subsidy removal effects on the poor.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent IMF mission statement with specific macro-fiscal and social-protection judgments tied to 2022 conditions.
evidence.period_fit: November 2022 mission statement squarely within target-year assessment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partially attributable to Buhari-era fiscal and monetary choices, but the IMF also notes external price shocks and broader macro constraints.
contrary_evidence: IMF recommendations are not proof of noncompliance or of intent.
Some inflation pressures came from global and war-related shocks.

evidence.claim: NBS reported that Nigeria's headline inflation rate was 21.34% in December 2022, up 5.72 percentage points from December 2021, with a month-on-month increase of 1.71% in December 2022.
evidence.title: CPI and Inflation Report December 2022
evidence.excerpt: NBS reported that Nigeria's headline inflation rate was 21.34% in December 2022, up 5.72 percentage points from December 2021, with a month-on-month increase of 1.71% in December 2022.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official national price statistics with a clear target-period release and standard methodology.
evidence.period_fit: Exact target-period inflation data released immediately after year-end 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Macro outcome only; attributable in part to federal policy but also to external shocks and inherited conditions.
contrary_evidence: Inflation data reflect multiple shocks, not only presidential choices.
A single monthly print does not capture distributional policy quality.

evidence.claim: NBS reported that 73.6% of working-age Nigerians were employed in Q4 2022, but 36.4% of employed persons worked fewer than 40 hours per week, underemployment was 13.7%, and short-hours work was most common among women, people with lower education, young people, and rural residents.
evidence.title: Nigeria Labour Force Survey Q4 2022 & Q1 2023
evidence.excerpt: NBS reported that 73.6% of working-age Nigerians were employed in Q4 2022, but 36.4% of employed persons worked fewer than 40 hours per week, underemployment was 13.7%, and short-hours work was most common among women, people with lower education, young people, and rural residents.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official labor market survey with concrete distributional breakdowns and a national sample-based methodology.
evidence.period_fit: The report explicitly covers Q4 2022 and Q1 2023, with the Q4 2022 figures relevant to the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Macro labor-market conditions are only partly attributable to Buhari; structural informality and shocks are major confounders.
contrary_evidence: Employment statistics do not directly measure well-being or job quality beyond hours worked.
The report spans two quarters and a transition into 2023.

unresolved_gaps: Direct 2022 ruler-attributed existential-risk choice under Buhari's own authority
Independent corroboration of the HEU-to-LEU conversion and other nuclear-security claims
Independent evidence of actual conflict-management effect from Buhari's Ukraine/ECOWAS diplomacy
Direct documentary support for the contested Lake Chad weapons claim or any concrete cross-border security outcome
More precise chain-of-command and federal-versus-state attribution for abuses and remedies
More direct evidence on Buhari's personal role in media and protest restrictions, beyond security-service and state-level actions
Independent implementation evidence for the 2022 Electoral Act and related reforms
More household-level and distributional evidence on the effects of subsidy, naira redesign, and fiscal choices
Cleaner evidence on whether economic appointees were selected for competence versus loyalty
Independent outcome evaluation of school feeding, BHCPF, rotavirus rollout, and related social programs
Subnational delivery and attribution, especially for north-south and rural-urban differences
Direct evidence on assets, beneficial ownership, gifts, campaign finance, or family enrichment
More independent evidence on truthfulness, correction, and acceptance of scrutiny
Better separation of Buhari's personal conduct from broader authoritarian or state-level behavior
Audited completion data for major projects and service-delivery claims
Independent evidence that coordination bodies and new appointments changed implementation quality

run_provenance.source_mix_note: Rich source metadata and chapter-specific reviewer exclusions were preserved during deterministic conversion.
